topic.subject: science
topic.title: Force and pressure
topic.scope: force as push or pull, contact and non-contact forces, effects of force, pressure and area, liquid and atmospheric pressure

nodes.name: Forces in same direction add up
Opposite forces subtract for net force
Force can change speed or direction
Gravity acts on all objects with mass
Pressure equals Force divided by Area
Atmosphere exerts pressure in all directions

misconceptions.statement: Force is something an object 'has' or 'contains' like an ingredient.
misconceptions.why: Students observe moving objects and think the force is inside them keeping them going.
misconceptions.fix: Force is not a property of one object; it is an interaction between at least two objects.

probe.question: If a ball is rolling on a floor, does it 'carry' force with it?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it has force which is why it keeps moving.

misconceptions.root_belief: force is an internal property of moving objects

misconceptions.statement: If an object is at rest, there are no forces acting on it.
misconceptions.why: Students only associate force with visible movement or change.
misconceptions.fix: Objects at rest often have multiple forces acting on them (like gravity and normal force) that cancel each other out.

probe.question: A book is lying still on a table. Are any forces acting on it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the book is not moving.

misconceptions.statement: Only living things like humans or animals can exert a force.
misconceptions.why: In everyday life, 'force' is often used as a synonym for effort or will.
misconceptions.fix: Non-living things like a table, a spring, or the ground can also exert forces.

probe.question: When you lean against a wall, does the wall exert a force on you?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the wall is an object and cannot push back.

misconceptions.statement: Friction only acts on objects that are already moving.
misconceptions.why: Students think friction is just the 'rubbing' they feel during motion.
misconceptions.fix: Friction also acts on stationary objects (static friction) to prevent them from starting to move.

probe.question: You try to push a heavy box but it doesn't move. Is friction acting?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because there is no rubbing or movement yet.

misconceptions.root_belief: friction is a result of motion only

misconceptions.statement: Gravity only acts on objects when they are falling through the air.
misconceptions.why: Students see gravity's effect most clearly when an object is dropped.
misconceptions.fix: Gravity acts on all objects at all times, whether they are falling, flying, or sitting on the ground.

probe.question: Does gravity act on a chair sitting on the floor?
probe.wrong_answer: No, gravity only starts working when the chair falls.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Pressure and Force are exactly the same thing.
misconceptions.why: The words are used interchangeably in common conversation.
misconceptions.fix: Force is a push or pull, while pressure is how that force is spread over a specific area.

probe.question: If you use a sharp needle instead of a blunt finger to push a balloon, why does it pop?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the needle has more force.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: A larger area always results in more pressure.
misconceptions.why: Students often associate 'larger' or 'more' with a greater effect.
misconceptions.fix: Pressure is inversely proportional to area; for the same force, a larger area results in less pressure.

probe.question: Why do heavy trucks have many wide tires?
probe.wrong_answer: To increase the pressure on the road so they don't slip.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Liquid pressure only acts downwards towards the bottom of the container.
misconceptions.why: Students relate liquid pressure to the weight of the water, which pulls down.
misconceptions.fix: Liquids exert pressure in all directions—sideways and upwards too—at any given depth.

probe.question: If you poke a hole in the side of a water bottle, why does water come out?
probe.wrong_answer: Because gravity pulls it down, not because of side pressure.

misconceptions.statement: Air cannot exert pressure because it is weightless and invisible.
misconceptions.why: Air feels like 'nothing' to students, and they don't feel the weight of the atmosphere.
misconceptions.fix: Air has mass and weight; the huge column of air above us exerts a large pressure in all directions.

probe.question: Why does a suction cup stick to a wall?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it has glue or it is sticky, not because of air.

misconceptions.root_belief: invisible things have no physical properties

misconceptions.statement: We don't feel atmospheric pressure because it is very weak.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that if they don't feel a sensation, the magnitude must be zero or low.
misconceptions.fix: Atmospheric pressure is very high, but we don't feel it because the pressure inside our bodies balances it.

probe.question: Is the air pressure on your head more than, less than, or equal to the weight of an elephant?
probe.wrong_answer: Much less, because I would be crushed otherwise.

misconceptions.root_belief: human sensation is the measure of magnitude

misconceptions.statement: If two people push an object from opposite sides, the object must stop moving.
misconceptions.why: Students think 'opposite' always means 'cancellation' regardless of the magnitude.
misconceptions.fix: The object only stops or stays still if the two opposite forces are equal in magnitude.

probe.question: A strong man pushes a box left and a child pushes it right. What happens?
probe.wrong_answer: The box stays still because they are pushing from opposite sides.

misconceptions.statement: Magnetic force only works if the magnet is touching the object.
misconceptions.why: Most forces students experience (pushing, pulling) require physical contact.
misconceptions.fix: Magnetic, electrostatic, and gravitational forces are non-contact forces that act through a distance.

probe.question: Can a magnet move a paperclip without touching it?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it must touch the clip to give it force.
